title: Ultraviolet diversity of Little Red Dots as a probe for direct-collapse black hole ages
comment: 11 pages, 4 figures. arXiv admin note: substantial text overlap with arXiv:2508.14897
summary: Little Red Dots (LRDs) uncovered by the James Webb Space Telescope have been proposed as candidate galaxies hosting embedded accreting direct-collapse black holes (DCBHs), yet the relative ultraviolet (UV) emission of their host galaxy remains highly uncertain and diverse across the population. Using a large-scale cosmological hydrodynamical simulation from the MELIORA suite, we investigate the contribution of PopIII stars and accreting DCBHs in LRD candidates at $z>8.5$, in the rest-frame $0.2-0.6~μ\mathrm{m}$ band. We find that the UV emission from the host galaxy evolves rapidly over the first $\sim 30~\mathrm{Myr}$ following DCBH formation, reflecting the build-up of stellar mass and metal enrichment. This evolution consists of a rapid transition from initially BH-dominated systems, with negligible stellar mass, low metallicity, and high accretion rates, to progressively more developed hosts in which rapid star formation enhances the UV output and metallicity increases. After $\sim 30~\mathrm{Myr}$, the stellar continuum typically overwhelms the accreting DCBH contribution, producing bluer colours and more extended stellar distributions. As a result, UV-bright LRDs are predicted to host older DCBHs, have higher gas-phase metallicities, lower BH-to-stellar mass ratios, and lower Eddington ratios. The short-lived nature of the LRD phase places strong constraints on their emergence over cosmic time. Overall, our results suggest that DCBH ages can be constrained from the host galaxy contribution to the UV-optical spectrum of LRDs, relative to that of the accreting DCBH, and support the picture in which a DCBH evolutionary sequence is systematically encoded in emission line properties, gas-phase metallicities, and accretion states.

AI.tldr: Using cosmological simulations, the paper shows that Little Red Dots (LRDs) at z>8.5 evolve rapidly from accreting direct-collapse black hole (DCBH)-dominated systems to host galaxy-dominated UV emission within ~30 Myr, with older DCBHs producing UV-bright LRDs with higher metallicity, lower BH-to-stellar mass ratios, and lower Eddington ratios.
AI.motivation: To investigate the relative UV emission contributions of host galaxies versus accreting DCBHs in LRD candidates at z>8.5, and to understand the evolutionary sequence encoded in their observable properties.
AI.method: Large-scale cosmological hydrodynamical simulation from the MELIORA suite, analyzing PopIII stars and accreting DCBHs in LRD candidates at z>8.5 in the rest-frame 0.2-0.6 μm band.
AI.result: UV emission evolves rapidly over the first ~30 Myr post-DCBH formation. Systems transition from BH-dominated (negligible stellar mass, low metallicity, high accretion) to host-dominated (rapid star formation enhances UV output, higher metallicity). After ~30 Myr, stellar continuum overwhelms DCBH contribution, producing bluer colors and more extended stellar distributions. UV-bright LRDs host older DCBHs with higher gas-phase metallicities, lower BH-to-stellar mass ratios, and lower Eddington ratios.
AI.conclusion: DCBH ages can be constrained from host galaxy UV-optical contributions relative to the accreting DCBH. A DCBH evolutionary sequence is systematically encoded in emission line properties, gas-phase metallicities, and accretion states. The LRD phase is short-lived, placing strong constraints on their cosmic emergence.

title: Eigenvalue formulation of Stochastic Inflation and application to large perturbation generating inflationary features
summary: Stochastic inflation is a powerful technique for calculating the probability distribution function (PDF) of large inflationary perturbations, which may collapse to form Primordial Black Holes. The PDF, $P({\cal N})$, of the stochastic number of e-folds, ${\cal N}$, satisfies an adjoint Fokker-Planck Equation. We develop a new self-contained eigenvalue technique which can be used to determine $P({\cal N})$. First we apply this method to the simple case of quantum diffusion along a flat potential without any classical drift. We recover the expression for the PDF that has previously been found using characteristic functions, with an exponential tail. We also identify an intermediate regime between the peak and the exponential tail of the PDF, which has not been emphasized in earlier studies, where it exhibits a power-law behaviour, $P({\cal N}) \propto {\cal N}^{-3/2}$. Finally we apply the method to constant drift inflation, in the narrow- and broad-well limits. In the narrow-well limit, there is an analytic solution and the PDF is similar to the drift-free case, with a mildly suppressed tail. In the broad-well limit, determining the full set of eigenvalues and eigenfunctions requires a piecewise construction of the spectrum, and the broad-well PDF is qualitatively different, with an enhanced peak and a strongly suppressed tail.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a new eigenvalue technique for solving the adjoint Fokker-Planck Equation in stochastic inflation to compute the PDF of the number of e-folds. The method reveals a power-law intermediate regime ($P(\mathcal{N}) \propto \mathcal{N}^{-3/2}$) for drift-free diffusion, and is extended to constant drift inflation in narrow- and broad-well limits, showing qualitatively different PDF behaviors.
AI.motivation: To provide a self-contained eigenvalue-based method for calculating the PDF of stochastic e-folds in inflation, improving upon existing techniques and enabling analysis of previously underexplored PDF regimes.
AI.method: The authors develop an eigenvalue technique to solve the adjoint Fokker-Planck Equation for the PDF of the stochastic number of e-folds. They apply it to (1) quantum diffusion on a flat potential (drift-free case), (2) narrow-well constant drift, and (3) broad-well constant drift, using piecewise spectral construction for the latter.
AI.result: For drift-free diffusion, they recover the known exponential tail and newly identify a power-law intermediate regime $P(\mathcal{N}) \propto \mathcal{N}^{-3/2}$. In the narrow-well limit, the PDF is similar to drift-free with mildly suppressed tail. In the broad-well limit, the PDF is qualitatively different with enhanced peak and strongly suppressed tail.
AI.conclusion: The eigenvalue technique is a viable self-contained method for stochastic inflation PDFs, revealing rich structure (power-law regime) not previously emphasized, and showing that well geometry qualitatively shapes the PDF behavior.

title: 21cmEMUv3: a hybrid diffusion-LSTM emulator of 21cmFAST summary observables
summary: We are witnessing a surge in observations of the cosmic dawn (CD) and epoch of reionisation (EoR), driving an increasing demand for fast and robust theoretical interpretation frameworks. In response, machine learning (ML), and emulation in particular, has emerged as a powerful approach to accelerate and enhance inference pipelines. In this work, we present 21cmEMUv3, an emulator trained on 21cmFASTv3 simulations that model both atomically and molecularly cooling galaxies. 21cmEMUv3 is conditioned on $σ_8$ and ten astrophysical parameters to produce seven summary observables: (i) the cylindrical 21cm power spectrum (PS), emulated for the first time at such high resolution and accuracy across a wide redshift range of $z \sim$ 6--30; (ii) the spherically-averaged 21cm PS; (iii) the mean neutral fraction of the intergalactic medium (IGM); (iv) the mean 21cm spin temperature; (v) the global 21cm signal; (vi) the ultraviolet (UV) luminosity functions (LFs); and (vii) the Thomson scattering optical depth. Notably, the cylindrical 21cm PS is emulated via score-based diffusion, while the remaining six summaries are emulated via long-short term memory (LSTM) networks, all achieving sub-percent median accuracy. We use the emulator to reinterpret current 21cm PS upper limits from HERA, for the first time using state-of-the-art hydrodynamical simulations to inform priors on star formation inside molecularly cooling galaxies. We find that our inferred soft-band X-ray luminosity per unit star formation rate is consistent with extrapolations of high-mass X-ray binaries to the low-metallicity regimes expected in the first galaxies, excluding values below $10^{39.2}$ erg s$^{-1}M^{-1}_\odot \rm{yr}$ at $95\%$ confidence. Finally, we produce forecasts for the detection of the cosmic 21cm PS with the Square Kilometre Array for different array configurations. The 21cmEMU package is publicly available.

AI.tldr: 21cmEMUv3 is a machine learning emulator trained on 21cmFASTv3 simulations that predicts seven summary observables of cosmic dawn and reionisation (including cylindrical 21cm PS via diffusion, and others via LSTM) with sub-percent accuracy. It is used to reinterpret HERA upper limits and produce SKA forecasts.
AI.motivation: The increasing volume of cosmic dawn and EoR observations demands fast and robust theoretical interpretation frameworks, motivating the development of ML-based emulators to accelerate inference pipelines.
AI.method: The emulator is trained on 21cmFASTv3 simulations (atomic + molecularly cooling galaxies), conditioned on σ₈ and ten astrophysical parameters. Cylindrical 21cm power spectrum is emulated via score-based diffusion; the other six summaries (spherical 21cm PS, mean neutral fraction, spin temperature, global 21cm signal, UV LFs, Thomson optical depth) via LSTM networks.
AI.result: All seven summary observables achieve sub-percent median accuracy. Reinterpretation of HERA upper limits constrains soft-band X-ray luminosity per SFR to >10³⁹·² erg s⁻¹M⊙⁻¹yr at 95% confidence, consistent with high-mass X-ray binary extrapolations. SKA forecasts are produced for different array configurations.
AI.conclusion: 21cmEMUv3 provides a fast, accurate, and publicly available framework for interpreting current and future 21cm observations, enabling robust inference of astrophysical parameters during the cosmic dawn and EoR.

title: Constraining Extragalactic Proper Motion with Gaia Astrometry
summary: The Solar System's secular motion with respect to the cosmic microwave background (CMB) rest frame is inferred from the CMB dipole and should induce a tiny, coherent apparent drift in the positions of nearby galaxies, referred to as the extragalactic proper motion. We test the feasibility of a purely geometric measurement of this effect by combining Gaia DR2 and DR3 astrometry with low-redshift spectroscopic galaxy catalogs to build a large, full-sky sample of $67,173$ galaxies. Although we do not obtain a statistically significant detection of the expected dipole signal, we place the tightest constraint to date on the extragalactic proper motion $\barπ$. Using galaxies with comoving distance $D>5 {\, \rm Mpc}$, we also place the tightest constraints on cosmic extragalactic proper motion $\barπ_{\rm cosmic}$, with uncertainty $\sim 10\times$ the measured CMB dipole value. Our $1σ$ uncertainty on the near field extragalactic proper motion $\barπ_{\rm nf}$ is approximately $\sim 1.3\times$ the expected CMB measurement, demonstrating that Gaia astrometry is approaching the sensitivity required for a direct detection of near field Hubble constant in future releases.

AI.tldr: This paper tests the feasibility of measuring the Solar System's secular motion relative to the CMB rest frame (extragalactic proper motion) using Gaia DR2/DR3 astrometry combined with low-redshift spectroscopic galaxy catalogs. Using 67,173 galaxies, the authors do not achieve a statistically significant detection but place the tightest constraints to date on this effect, with uncertainty approaching the expected CMB dipole signal for near-field measurements.
AI.motivation: The Solar System's motion relative to the CMB rest frame should induce a coherent apparent drift in the positions of nearby galaxies (extragalactic proper motion). A purely geometric measurement of this effect could provide independent constraints on the Hubble constant and test fundamental physics, but has not been convincingly detected.
AI.method: Combined Gaia DR2 and DR3 astrometry with low-redshift spectroscopic galaxy catalogs to construct a full-sky sample of 67,173 galaxies. Analyzed the proper motion dipole signal expected from the Solar System's CMB-frame motion.
AI.result: No statistically significant detection of the expected dipole signal. However, placed the tightest constraints to date on extragalactic proper motion (π̄). For cosmic extragalactic proper motion (π̄_cosmic), achieved uncertainty ~10× the measured CMB dipole value. For near-field extragalactic proper motion (π̄_nf), achieved 1σ uncertainty ~1.3× the expected CMB measurement.
AI.conclusion: Gaia astrometry is approaching the sensitivity required for direct detection of near-field extragalactic proper motion and potentially the Hubble constant in future releases, though a clear detection remains elusive.

title: The sound of dynamical dark energy and modified gravity
summary: Different candidate models are able to reproduce the dynamical dark energy signal preferred by combinations of recent distance measurements. These models may be distinguished by the behavior of their perturbations, which are controlled by the effective sound speed $c_s^2(k,a)$. To explore correlations between the dark energy sound speed and perturbative behavior, we test modified gravity (MG) scenarios in which the dark energy equation of state and sound speed determine modifications to the clustering of matter. We investigate the impact of varying the dark energy sound speed on several cosmological quantities in both General Relativity (GR) and MG. We constrain the dark energy and modified gravity parameters using measurements of the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) from Planck PR4, type Ia supernova luminosity distances (SN) from Pantheon+, Baryon Acoustic Oscillations (BAO) from DESI DR2, and cosmic shear from DES-Y3. Using the combination of CMB+BAO+SN, we find that, in the MG scenarios, the preference for dynamical dark energy is correlated with deviations from GR over redshifts $z < 2$ at over 95\% confidence level. The significance of these deviations is not degraded when considering a dynamical or superluminal sound speed, but vanishes if we assume a cosmological constant. The inclusion of cosmic shear and CMB lensing data significantly shifts the constraints towards GR. Our framework enables the exploration of modified gravity models using the dark energy sound speed as a physically meaningful free parameter.

AI.tldr: The paper explores correlations between dark energy sound speed and modified gravity, finding that MG scenarios show preference for dynamical dark energy correlated with deviations from GR at >95% confidence for z<2, with constraints shifting toward GR when cosmic shear and CMB lensing data are included.
AI.motivation: To explore correlations between the dark energy sound speed and perturbative behavior in modified gravity scenarios, and to understand how different candidate models reproducing dynamical dark energy signals can be distinguished by their perturbation properties.
AI.method: Tested modified gravity scenarios where dark energy equation of state and sound speed determine modifications to matter clustering; constrained parameters using Planck PR4 CMB, Pantheon+ SN, DESI DR2 BAO, and DES-Y3 cosmic shear data.
AI.result: MG scenarios show a preference for dynamical dark energy correlated with deviations from GR over z<2 at >95% CL. Significance persists with dynamical/superluminal sound speed but vanishes with a cosmological constant. Adding cosmic shear and CMB lensing shifts constraints toward GR.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables exploration of modified gravity models using dark energy sound speed as a physically meaningful free parameter, showing that current data can distinguish between MG and GR under different sound speed assumptions.

title: Spectroscopic characterization of Young Stellar Populations and their Feedback in NGC 5253
comment: 24 pages, 11 figures, 5 tables, Accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: We present the spectroscopic analysis of FUV observations taken with the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) Cosmic Origins Spectrograph (COS) targeting young massive clusters in the nearby, metal-poor, blue compact dwarf galaxy NGC 5253. We characterize the stellar populations observed across seven COS pointings and report on their inferred physical parameters, age, metallicity, mass, and reddening values. Comparison between our spectroscopic ages and those inferred using photometric methods show that the former are preferentially younger. We also investigate the impact of these young massive clusters on their surrounding ISM. Using Very Large Telescope/MUSE optical observations and matching the size of the COS aperture, we measured outflow velocities of the ionized gas along the line of sight of the COS pointing with values ranging from $\sim$125-300 km s$^{-1}$. We report on strong statistically-significant correlations between the outflow velocities and the stellar ages, masses, and total mechanical luminosity primarily driven by supernovae (SNe) as derived from our full-spectrum fitting analysis. Although theoretical models predict a delayed injection of mechanical energy and momentum in low-metallicity environments ($<$0.4 Z$_{\odot}$), our study shows that in this particular system (Z$\sim$ 0.3 Z$_{\odot}$), feedback from SNe appears evident at the nominal $>$ 5 Myr ages, with no apparent delay. One possible explanation is that the decrease and suppression of mechanical feedback due to SNe explosions might be dominant at even lower metallicities than those observed in NGC 5253.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes HST/COS FUV spectroscopy of young massive clusters in the metal-poor dwarf galaxy NGC 5253, characterizing their stellar populations (ages, metallicities, masses, reddening). Spectroscopic ages are younger than photometric ones. Using VLT/MUSE data, outflow velocities of ionized gas (125-300 km/s) correlate strongly with stellar ages, masses, and SN-driven mechanical luminosity. Feedback from SNe is evident at >5 Myr without delay, contrary to theoretical predictions for low-metallicity environments.
AI.motivation: To characterize young massive clusters in a metal-poor (Z~0.3 Z☉) blue compact dwarf galaxy via FUV spectroscopy, and to investigate the impact of these clusters on the surrounding interstellar medium through outflow velocity measurements, testing theoretical predictions about delayed mechanical feedback at low metallicity.
AI.method: HST/COS FUV spectroscopy across seven pointings in NGC 5253 to infer stellar population parameters (age, metallicity, mass, reddening) via full-spectrum fitting. VLT/MUSE optical observations matched to COS aperture size to measure ionized gas outflow velocities along each line of sight. Statistical correlations were computed between outflow velocities and inferred stellar parameters.
AI.result: Spectroscopic ages are preferentially younger than photometric ages. Outflow velocities range ~125-300 km/s. Strong statistically-significant correlations exist between outflow velocities and stellar ages, masses, and SN-driven mechanical luminosity. SNe feedback appears evident at >5 Myr with no apparent delay, contrary to theoretical models predicting delayed injection in low-metallicity environments.
AI.conclusion: In NGC 5253 (Z~0.3 Z☉), SNe feedback is observed without delay at ages >5 Myr, contradicting models predicting delayed mechanical feedback at metallicities <0.4 Z☉. The suppression of mechanical feedback may dominate at even lower metallicities than those found in this system.

title: Decaying Dark Matter as a Possible Solution for Cosmological Tensions
summary: Large-scale structure measurements have revealed persistent tensions between early- and late-time cosmological probes, most notably the long-standing discrepancy in the structure-growth parameter $S_8$. In this work, we explore how a model including decaying dark matter (DDM) can alleviate this tension by suppressing the growth of matter fluctuations at late times. Specifically, we consider a neutrinophilic decay channel in which a heavy dark matter particle $χ$ slowly decays into a Standard Model neutrino and a light invisible fermion, $χ\rightarrow ν+ φ$, modifying both the background evolution and the clustering of structure. Using the DES Year~1 redshift distributions, we construct a baseline matter power spectrum and compute the galaxy-galaxy, shear-shear, and galaxy-shear angular power spectra under both $Λ$CDM and DDM-inspired scenarios. We find that slow dark matter decay produces a scale-dependent suppression of clustering that remains consistent with DES measurements while naturally shifting the predicted structure amplitude toward the lower values favored by weak lensing surveys. Our results suggest that decaying dark matter is a compelling and physically motivated framework for addressing the $S_8$ tension.

AI.tldr: This paper explores how decaying dark matter (DDM) with a neutrinophilic decay channel ($χ\rightarrow ν+ φ$) can alleviate the $S_8$ tension between early- and late-time cosmological probes by suppressing matter fluctuations at late times, and shows consistency with DES Year 1 measurements.
AI.motivation: Persistent tensions in the structure-growth parameter $S_8$ between early- and late-time cosmological probes motivate exploring beyond-$Λ$CDM physics to resolve the discrepancy.
AI.method: The authors consider a DDM model where heavy dark matter decays into a neutrino and a light invisible fermion. Using DES Year 1 redshift distributions, they compute galaxy-galaxy, shear-shear, and galaxy-shear angular power spectra under both $Λ$CDM and DDM scenarios.
AI.result: Slow dark matter decay produces a scale-dependent suppression of clustering consistent with DES measurements, shifting the predicted structure amplitude toward the lower values favored by weak lensing surveys.
AI.conclusion: Decaying dark matter is a compelling and physically motivated framework for addressing the $S_8$ tension.

title: Vision-Language Model Ensembles Achieve Human-Expert Accuracy for Galaxy Merger Classification
comment: This work used LLMs as research assistants for code development, statistical analysis, and drafting under close human supervision; the workflow is described in Appendix A. Submitted to the Astronomical Journal
summary: We present a proof-of-concept study demonstrating that an ensemble of Vision--Language Models (VLMs) combined using a Bayesian statistical framework can classify galaxy merger morphologies with accuracy comparable to trained human experts. We deploy 15 VLM classifier configurations, spanning four model architectures (Gemma-4 E2B, Gemma-4 E4B, Qwen2.5-VL, and Qwen3-VL) tested with up to four prompt engineering strategies each. We evaluate their performance against a truth-known sample of 41 VELA+SUNRISE mock galaxy images from Lambrides et al. 2021. The VLM ensemble achieves 83.3\% accuracy on confident classifications (merger probability $p_{\rm M} \ge 0.8$ or $p_{\rm M} \le 0.2$), with 5 misclassified galaxies. The ensemble recovers the population merger fraction to within $0.66σ$ of the truth ($f_{\rm M} = 0.52 \pm 0.09$ vs.\ true value of 0.585). Bayesian weighting improves overall accuracy by 17.1 percentage points over simple majority voting, with sensitivity improving by 29.2 percentage points. The VLM ensemble produces 5 misclassified galaxies (2 false positives, 3 false negatives), comparable to the 6 misclassifications (5 false positives, 1 false negative) reported for human classifiers by Lambrides et al. 2021. The apparent differences in error profiles are not statistically significant given the sample size of 41 galaxies. VLMs also produce more moderate per-galaxy merger probability distributions (27\% uncertain) than the more polarized human distributions (15\% uncertain), though this difference is also consistent with statistical fluctuation. These results establish VLMs as scalable, reproducible alternatives to human classifiers within a Bayesian probabilistic merger-fraction framework, with direct applications to large galaxy samples from current and future surveys.

AI.tldr: A Bayesian ensemble of 15 Vision-Language Models (4 architectures, multiple prompts) classifies galaxy merger morphologies with accuracy comparable to trained human experts, achieving 83.3% accuracy on confident classifications and recovering the population merger fraction to within 0.66σ of truth on 41 VELA+SUNRISE mock galaxy images.
AI.motivation: To establish Vision-Language Models (VLMs) as scalable, reproducible alternatives to human classifiers for galaxy merger morphology classification, enabling analysis of large galaxy samples from current and future surveys where human expert classification is impractical.
AI.method: An ensemble of 15 VLM classifier configurations (Gemma-4 E2B, Gemma-4 E4B, Qwen2.5-VL, Qwen3-VL) with up to 4 prompt engineering strategies each, combined using a Bayesian statistical framework, evaluated on 41 VELA+SUNRISE mock galaxy images with known merger truth labels.
AI.result: The VLM ensemble achieves 83.3% accuracy on confident classifications, with 5 misclassified galaxies (2 false positives, 3 false negatives), comparable to the 6 misclassifications (5 false positives, 1 false negative) from human classifiers. Bayesian weighting improves accuracy by 17.1 percentage points over majority voting. The ensemble recovers the merger fraction (f_M = 0.52 ± 0.09) vs. true value of 0.585 (within 0.66σ).
AI.conclusion: VLMs, when combined in a Bayesian ensemble, serve as scalable and reproducible alternatives to human experts for galaxy merger classification, with statistically comparable error profiles and more moderate (less polarized) probability distributions, suitable for large-scale survey applications.

title: Interacting dark energy constraints from Fermi GRBs and Pantheon+ SNe Ia with full GRB covariance
summary: The standard $Λ$CDM model faces long-standing theoretical and observational problems, such as the Hubble tension, which motivate extensions beyond $Λ$CDM, including interacting dark energy (IDE). Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) are precise probes of the late-time expansion history, while gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) can extend distance measurements to higher redshifts. However, GRB cosmology depends on the calibration of luminosity relations, the covariance treatment, and the intrinsic scatter. In this work, we use 15 years of Fermi/GBM long-GRB observations and Pantheon+ SNe Ia to test whether current distance data provide evidence in favor of IDE models over $Λ$CDM. We compare four flat models: $Λ$CDM, $w$CDM, IDE-$ρ_{\rm de}$, and IDE-$ρ_{\rm c}$. The GRB covariance is constructed by propagating the Amati-relation calibration covariance, and the GRB intrinsic scatter is sampled as a nuisance parameter. A diagonal GRB covariance is also considered as a robustness test. With the full GRB covariance, both the GOLD and FULL samples give $H_0\simeq 72.8~{\rm km~s^{-1}~Mpc^{-1}}$ in $Λ$CDM. The IDE models do not improve the fit enough to compensate for their extra parameters, and the BIC favors the simpler $Λ$CDM model. The diagonal-covariance test gives the same model-selection conclusion, although it changes the fitted GRB intrinsic scatter. We conclude that, for the two interaction forms considered here and at the present level of GRB systematics, current GRB and Pantheon+ data do not provide evidence for interacting dark energy. Current GRBs mainly provide a high-redshift extension of the Hubble diagram and test the shape of the expansion history.

AI.tldr: Using 15 years of Fermi/GBM GRBs and Pantheon+ SNe Ia, the study finds that interacting dark energy (IDE) models do not improve fits enough to be favored over ΛCDM; Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) prefers the simpler ΛCDM model.
AI.motivation: The ΛCDM model faces theoretical and observational issues (e.g., Hubble tension), motivating extensions such as interacting dark energy (IDE). The paper aims to test whether current distance data from GRBs and SNe Ia provide evidence for IDE over ΛCDM.
AI.method: Four flat cosmological models (ΛCDM, wCDM, IDE-ρ_de, IDE-ρ_c) are compared using 15 years of Fermi/GBM long-GRB observations and Pantheon+ SNe Ia. GRB covariance is constructed from Amati-relation calibration covariance, with intrinsic scatter sampled as a nuisance parameter; a diagonal covariance test is also performed.
AI.result: With full GRB covariance, both GOLD and FULL samples yield H₀ ≈ 72.8 km/s/Mpc in ΛCDM. IDE models do not improve fit sufficiently to justify extra parameters; BIC favors ΛCDM. The diagonal-covariance test yields the same model-selection conclusion, though it changes fitted GRB intrinsic scatter.
AI.conclusion: For the two interaction forms considered and at the current level of GRB systematics, GRB and Pantheon+ data do not provide evidence for interacting dark energy. GRBs mainly serve as a high-redshift extension of the Hubble diagram to test the shape of the expansion history.

title: Non-detection of HC(S)SH: Estimating Upper Limits and Constraining Chemistry
comment: Accepted for publication in the Astrophysical Journal
summary: The search for dithioformic acid (t-HC(S)SH) in star-forming regions is crucial for understanding interstellar sulfur chemistry and addressing the 'missing sulfur' problem. Motivated by a recent claim of t-HC(S)SH detection in NGC 1333 IRAS 4A2, we independently reanalyzed the same ALMA dataset using comprehensive spectral and chemical modeling. We find no credible evidence for t-HC(S)SH: all reported transitions are fully accounted for by known, abundant molecules, with no unblended features unique to t-HC(S)SH. We critically reassess the reported detection, deriving stringent upper limits on the column density (N_t-HC(S)SH <= 4 x 10^14 cm^-2) and the fractional abundance (<= 1 x 10^-10 relative to H2). Our astrochemical models place these limits in context, showing the claimed detection likely results from spectral blending and inconsistent modeling assumptions. The non-detection aligns with chemical expectations given the rarity of complex and doubly sulfur-substituted molecules in hot corino environments. Furthermore, our analysis establishes a rigorous framework to guide future searches for sulfur-bearing species and highlights the critical importance of thorough line identification and modeling practices in astrochemistry.

AI.tldr: This paper reanalyzes ALMA observations of NGC 1333 IRAS 4A2 and finds no credible evidence for dithioformic acid (t-HC(S)SH), contradicting a previous detection claim. All reported transitions are explained by known molecules, and the authors derive stringent upper limits on column density and fractional abundance.
AI.motivation: To independently verify a claimed detection of dithioformic acid (t-HC(S)SH) in NGC 1333 IRAS 4A2, which is important for understanding interstellar sulfur chemistry and the 'missing sulfur' problem in star-forming regions.
AI.method: Reanalysis of the same ALMA dataset used in the original detection claim, employing comprehensive spectral and chemical modeling, along with critical reassessment of reported transitions and derivation of upper limits.
AI.result: No credible evidence for t-HC(S)SH was found; all reported transitions are fully accounted for by known abundant molecules with no unblended features unique to t-HC(S)SH. Stringent upper limits were derived: N_t-HC(S)SH ≤ 4×10^14 cm^-2 and fractional abundance ≤ 1×10^-10 relative to H2.
AI.conclusion: The claimed detection likely results from spectral blending and inconsistent modeling assumptions. The non-detection aligns with chemical expectations, and the study establishes a rigorous framework to guide future searches for sulfur-bearing species in astrochemistry.

title: Testing the cosmological principle with quasars
comment: 7 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables, version matched the publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: The inferred velocity is consistent at the 1.56 σ level with the value of 370 km/s from a purely kinematic interpretation of the CMB dipole. Based on the motion direction component analysis, we have not found any significant deviation from cosmological principle in current released quasars data. The cosmological principle posits that the universe is homogeneous and isotropic on the large scales. In history, the cosmological principle was confirmed by various cosmological observations from CMB to large scale structure. However, several new challenges to the cosmological principle were reported in recent years, particularly in radio observations from overdispersed radio source counts to quasars. Here, we firstly present studies on the peculiar velocity of large-scale anisotropy by measuring the dipole signal from the DESI DR1 catalogue with a sample of 1,176,570 quasars (0.8 < z < 3.0). Our analysis reveals the peculiar velocity of $|v| = 443.8 \pm 204.1$ km/s towards $(l, b) = (107.4^\circ \pm 86.8^\circ, 28.4^\circ \pm 45.2^\circ)$ in Galactic coordinates.The motion direction deviates from the CMB dipole (264.02$^\circ$, 48.253$^\circ$). The inferred velocity is consistent at the 1.56 $σ$ level with the value of 370 km/s from a purely kinematic interpretation of the CMB dipole. Based on the motion direction component analysis, we have not found any significant deviation from cosmological principle in current released quasars data.

AI.tldr: Using 1.17 million quasars from DESI DR1, the authors measure a peculiar velocity of 443.8 ± 204.1 km/s toward (l,b) = (107.4°, 28.4°), consistent with the CMB kinematic dipole at 1.56σ, and find no significant violation of the cosmological principle.
AI.motivation: To test the cosmological principle (large-scale homogeneity and isotropy) by measuring the peculiar velocity dipole from quasar number count data, responding to recent radio-based challenges to the standard cosmological model.
AI.method: Analyzed the DESI DR1 catalogue containing 1,176,570 quasars (0.8 < z < 3.0) and measured the dipole signal in their number count distribution to infer the peculiar velocity of large-scale anisotropy.
AI.result: Peculiar velocity |v| = 443.8 ± 204.1 km/s toward Galactic (l,b) = (107.4° ± 86.8°, 28.4° ± 45.2°). The direction deviates from the CMB dipole (264.02°, 48.253°), but the inferred velocity is consistent with the kinematic CMB dipole value of 370 km/s at 1.56σ.
AI.conclusion: Based on motion direction component analysis, no significant deviation from the cosmological principle is found in the current quasar data.

title: The cosmic ray ionization rate from H3+ observations can be overestimated due to neglect of time-dependent chemistry
summary: The cosmic ray ionization rate (CRIR) is a key parameter governing the physical, chemical and thermal evolution of the interstellar medium. The primary technique for measuring the CRIR in diffuse molecular clouds relies on observations of ${\rm H_3^+}$. Previous analyses of these observations have derived the CRIR under the assumption of steady-state chemistry. Here, we investigate the effect of time-dependent chemistry on the inferred CRIR from ${\rm H_3^+}$ observations. We perform 3D MHD simulations with coupled chemistry and driven turbulence. Following procedures similar to those used in the literature to analyze ${\rm H_3^+}$ observations, we conduct mock CRIR measurements by post-processing our simulations with different values of the CRIR to obtain steady-state abundances of ${\rm H_2}$ and ${\rm H_3^+}$. By comparing those with the abundances from time-dependent chemistry, we determine the best-fitting value of the CRIR. We find that the abundances of both ${\rm H_2}$ and ${\rm H_3^+}$ are higher in time-dependent chemistry simulations than in the steady-state case, especially in low-density regions. Furthermore, the inferred CRIR under the steady-state assumption is a factor of $\sim 2-5$ higher than the true CRIR, with a median value of $ζ_\mathrm{inferred}/ζ_\mathrm{true} \approx 3$. This bias increases with stronger magnetic fields, weaker FUV radiation fields, and stronger turbulence. Accounting for time-dependent chemistry, we report an average CRIR per ${\rm H_2}$ of $ζ_{H_2} = 2\times 10^{-17}~\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ from the ${\rm H_3^+}$ observations. The CRIR is consistent with a constant value over the column density range of $N=(2-6)\times10^{21}~\mathrm{cm^{-2}}$.

AI.tldr: Time-dependent chemistry causes the cosmic ray ionization rate (CRIR) inferred from H₃⁺ observations under steady-state assumptions to be overestimated by a factor of ~2–5 (median ~3). After accounting for this bias, the average CRIR per H₂ is ζ_H₂ = 2×10⁻¹⁷ s⁻¹, constant over column densities N = (2–6)×10²¹ cm⁻².
AI.motivation: The CRIR is a key parameter for interstellar medium evolution, but previous analyses of H₃⁺ observations assumed steady-state chemistry, potentially biasing the inferred CRIR. The authors aim to investigate the impact of time-dependent chemistry on these measurements.
AI.method: The authors perform 3D MHD simulations with coupled time-dependent chemistry and driven turbulence. They conduct mock CRIR measurements by post-processing simulations with various CRIR values to obtain steady-state H₂ and H₃⁺ abundances, then compare with time-dependent chemistry abundances to find the best-fitting CRIR.
AI.result: Time-dependent chemistry yields higher H₂ and H₃⁺ abundances than steady-state, especially at low densities. The steady-state assumption overestimates CRIR by ~2–5× (median ~3×). The bias increases with stronger magnetic fields, weaker FUV radiation, and stronger turbulence. The corrected average CRIR per H₂ is ζ_H₂ = 2×10⁻¹⁷ s⁻¹, constant across N = (2–6)×10²¹ cm⁻².
AI.conclusion: Time-dependent chemistry significantly biases CRIR measurements derived from H₃⁺ observations if steady-state chemistry is assumed. Accounting for this effect yields a lower, constant CRIR, providing a more accurate measurement of the cosmic ray ionization rate in diffuse molecular clouds.

title: Calibrating Self-Weighted Shear Estimation via Field Distortion
comment: Submitted to Research in Astronomy and Astrophysics. Welcome comments!
summary: Accurate cosmic shear measurement is the key to fully realize the scientific potential of large scale galaxy surveys. The Fourier\_Quad shear measurement method has been significantly developed to avoid biases caused by various factors, including the point spread function (PSF), photon noise, pixelation effect, selection effects, etc.. Shear statistics has also been optimized by using the PDF-SYM method (symmetrization of the Probability Distribution Function of the shear estimators) to achieve the minimal statistical error, without introducing systematic error. Nevertheless, the iterative nature of the PDF-SYM method makes it computationally expensive for massive datasets. To substantially improve efficiency, we introduce the Self-Weighted Shear Estimation (SWSE) method, which employs a specific self-weighting scheme to naturally suppress the shape noise as well as to balance the contributions from the bright and faint galaxies. Because SWSE is intrinsically biased, the primary focus of this work is to robustly evaluate whether the field-distortion test (FD test, a way to calibrate the shear bias on real data) can accurately recover and correct these inherent multiplicative and additive biases. Using both simulated and real survey data, we demonstrate that the FD test can successfully calibrate SWSE on galaxy-galaxy lensing measurements, enabling it to achieve statistical precision comparable to PDF-SYM. Our results establish the combination of FD test and SWSE as a robust shear estimation approach for forthcoming large-scale weak lensing surveys.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Self-Weighted Shear Estimation (SWSE) method to improve computational efficiency of cosmic shear measurement, and validates that the field-distortion (FD) test can successfully calibrate its inherent biases, making SWSE+FD a robust approach for large-scale weak lensing surveys.
AI.motivation: Accurate cosmic shear measurement is essential for large-scale galaxy surveys, but existing methods like PDF-SYM are computationally expensive due to iterative processing, creating a need for more efficient approaches without sacrificing accuracy.
AI.method: The authors propose the Self-Weighted Shear Estimation (SWSE) method, which uses a self-weighting scheme to suppress shape noise and balance contributions from bright and faint galaxies. They evaluate whether the field-distortion (FD) test can calibrate SWSE's inherent multiplicative and additive biases.
AI.result: Using both simulated and real survey data, the FD test successfully calibrates SWSE on galaxy-galaxy lensing measurements, achieving statistical precision comparable to PDF-SYM.
AI.conclusion: The combination of FD test and SWSE provides a robust and efficient shear estimation approach suitable for forthcoming large-scale weak lensing surveys.

title: Understanding the Broad-line Region of Active Galactic Nuclei with Photoionization. II. Slim disks, Self-shadowing, and BLR sizes
comment: 19 pages, 13 figures. Submitted to ApJ. Comments welcome!
summary: Reverberation-mapping (RM) measurements have revealed that high-accretion-rate active galactic nuclei (AGNs) systematically lie below the canonical broad-line region (BLR) radius - optical continuum luminosity (R-L) relation, exhibiting shorter lags than predicted for fixed 5100Åluminosity. The physical origin of these offsets remains debated. We investigate how accretion-flow structure and BLR cloud properties affect the emissivity-weighted BLR radius using analytic slim-disk SEDs and photoionization calculations on a two-dimensional axisymmetric grid. As the accretion rate approaches and exceeds the Eddington limit, geometric thickening of the inner disk produces anisotropic illumination and self-shadowing, reducing ionizing flux seen by low-latitude BLR clouds and flattening the R-L relation at high L/LEdd. Self-shadowing at high accretion rates reproduces the observed R-L trend in the RM AGN sample reasonably well, but this effect alone is insufficient to explain the observed lag offset in low-mass ($\sim10^{7}M_\odot$) systems with high accretion rates. Motivated by accretion-disk density scalings, we further explore models in which the BLR gas density increases toward lower black hole mass or higher accretion rate. We find that an accretion-rate-dependent BLR density enhancement further improves agreement with observed RM data, where the BLR gas density increases by a factor of 3-5 for one dex increase in $\dot{m}$. Variations in BLR opening angles produce a less important effect on BLR sizes. These results demonstrate that self-consistent modeling of accretion disk SED, BLR illumination and photoionization, and gas density variations can fully explain the observed distribution of AGNs in the BLR size - optical luminosity plane. This framework provides a physically motivated link between accretion-flow structure and BLR observables across a broad range of black-hole properties.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates why high-accretion-rate AGNs deviate from the standard BLR radius-luminosity relation, finding that self-shadowing from thickened inner accretion disks and accretion-rate-dependent BLR gas density increases can together explain the observed shorter lags, linking accretion-flow structure to BLR observables.
AI.motivation: To understand the physical origin of systematic offsets observed in reverberation-mapping measurements, where high-accretion-rate AGNs exhibit shorter BLR lags (smaller BLR radii) than predicted by the canonical R-L relation at fixed 5100Å luminosity.
AI.method: Used analytic slim-disk SEDs coupled with photoionization calculations on a 2D axisymmetric grid to model emissivity-weighted BLR radius. Explored effects of disk geometric thickening, self-shadowing, and accretion-rate-dependent BLR gas density on the R-L relation.
AI.result: Self-shadowing reproduces the overall R-L trend in RM AGN samples but fails to explain offsets in low-mass (~10^7 M⊙), high-accretion-rate systems. Adding an accretion-rate-dependent BLR density enhancement (factor 3-5 per dex increase in ṁ) significantly improves agreement with data. BLR opening angle variations have minor effects.
AI.conclusion: Self-consistent modeling of accretion disk SED, BLR illumination/photoionization, and gas density variations fully explains the observed AGN distribution in the BLR size-luminosity plane, providing a physically motivated link between accretion-flow structure and BLR observables.

title: Generative Diffusion Priors for 3D Mapping of the Dark Universe
summary: Reconstructing the three-dimensional distribution of dark matter from weak-lensing observations is a central but highly ill-posed inverse problem in cosmology. Unlike standard 3D reconstruction with multiple viewpoints, we observe the universe from a single line of sight, through noisy shape distortions of galaxies with uncertain distances, so meaningful recovery of the 3D matter field requires strong prior assumptions. Existing methods either produce point estimates with handcrafted priors or use neural ensembles for approximate Bayesian uncertainty, and struggle to capture the non-Gaussian, filamentary structure of the cosmic web. With the advent of new high-resolution cosmological simulations, we now have an alternative source of prior knowledge that captures the nonlinear statistics of structure formation with far greater fidelity than analytic prescriptions. We leverage these simulations to build a new dataset $\texttt{Conicus3D}$, which enables us to learn a data-driven diffusion-model prior capturing the full 3D distribution of dark matter structure across cosmic time. Building on recent plug-and-play approaches, we modify a diffusion-based posterior sampling scheme to the 3D weak-lensing setting, combining the learned prior with a differentiable physical forward model. On realistic simulations targeting a modern weak lensing survey, our approach yields substantially improved 2D and 3D reconstruction accuracy over baseline methods. Moreover, it produces posterior samples whose statistics closely track the underlying simulations, while remaining robust to moderate shifts in cosmology.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Conicus3D, a dataset and diffusion-model-based prior for 3D weak-lensing dark matter reconstruction, demonstrating improved accuracy and robust posterior sampling over existing methods on realistic survey simulations.
AI.motivation: 3D dark matter reconstruction from weak lensing is a severely ill-posed inverse problem with single line-of-sight observations and noisy data. Existing methods use handcrafted priors or neural ensembles that fail to capture the non-Gaussian, filamentary cosmic web structure, motivating the need for data-driven priors from high-resolution cosmological simulations.
AI.method: The authors build Conicus3D, a dataset from cosmological simulations, and train a diffusion-model prior on the full 3D dark matter distribution. They then adapt a plug-and-play diffusion-based posterior sampling scheme to the 3D weak-lensing setting by combining the learned prior with a differentiable physical forward model.
AI.result: On realistic simulations of a modern weak lensing survey, the approach yields substantially improved 2D and 3D reconstruction accuracy over baseline methods. The posterior samples closely match the statistics of the underlying simulations and remain robust to moderate shifts in cosmology.
AI.conclusion: Learned diffusion priors from simulations offer a powerful alternative to analytic prescriptions for 3D weak-lensing reconstruction, enabling both better point estimates and faithful uncertainty quantification that captures the nonlinear structure of the cosmic web.

title: The First Glimpse of Water Ice Absorption Map in the Milky Way
comment: 15 pages, 12 figures. Manuscript in second revision under review
summary: Interstellar ice plays a key role in the thermal evolution of the interstellar medium and in astrochemical pathways, yet its large-scale distribution remains poorly constrained. We use ALLWISE and 2MASS photometry to estimate water ice absorption in the $\Wi$/WISE band by correcting the observed colors for reddening and intrinsic stellar colors. This allows us to construct a first Milky Way water ice map. By varying input parameters, we test the stability of the method and identify the extinction law as the dominant source of uncertainty. Using synthetic photometry, we also quantify how different physical and observational parameters influence the $\Wi$ band water ice absorption. The strong correlation between the measurement from photometric method and spectroscopic water ice abundance confirms that the $\Wi$ band signature originates from the 3 $μ$m ice feature. We present the relationship between ice absorption in $\Wi$ band and water ice optical depth from theory and observations. Finally, we provide a preliminary Milky Way-scale map of water ice distribution.

AI.tldr: Using ALLWISE and 2MASS photometry, the authors construct the first Milky Way-wide map of water ice distribution by measuring 3 μm ice absorption in the W1 band, validating the method against spectroscopic data.
AI.motivation: Interstellar ice is crucial for thermal evolution and astrochemistry in the interstellar medium, but its large-scale distribution remains poorly constrained.
AI.method: The authors use ALLWISE and 2MASS photometry to estimate water ice absorption in the WISE W1 band by correcting observed colors for reddening and intrinsic stellar colors. They test stability via varying input parameters and use synthetic photometry to quantify the influence of physical and observational parameters.
AI.result: A strong correlation between the photometric measurement and spectroscopic water ice abundance confirms the W1 band signature originates from the 3 μm ice feature. They derive the relationship between ice absorption in W1 band and water ice optical depth, and produce a preliminary Milky Way-scale water ice map.
AI.conclusion: The photometric method effectively traces water ice on Galactic scales, with extinction law identified as the dominant uncertainty. The resulting map provides the first large-scale view of water ice distribution across the Milky Way.

title: A short review on Quintom dark energy theory
summary: In this paper, we provide a short review on the Quintom dark energy theory. Firstly, we discuss the No-Go theorem associated with dynamical dark energy, then present some examples of models in which the equation of state (EoS) evolves with time and can cross $w=-1$ . Secondly, we discuss the bouncing universe and emergent universe with Quintom matter. Finally, we discuss the possibility of studying the nature of dark energy by measuring the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) polarization rotation angle.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews Quintom dark energy theory, discussing the No-Go theorem for dynamical dark energy, models with EoS crossing w=-1, bouncing/emergent universes with Quintom matter, and CMB polarization rotation as a probe of dark energy.
AI.motivation: To provide a concise review of Quintom dark energy theory, addressing the limitations of single-field dark energy models (No-Go theorem) and exploring alternative cosmological scenarios that allow the equation of state to cross the phantom divide (w=-1).
AI.method: A theoretical review approach: (1) Discusses the No-Go theorem for dynamical dark energy and presents models enabling EoS crossing w=-1; (2) Examines bouncing and emergent universe scenarios with Quintom matter; (3) Proposes using CMB polarization rotation angle measurements to study dark energy properties.
AI.result: Identifies that Quintom models can circumvent the No-Go theorem and allow w=-1 crossing; demonstrates that Quintom matter supports bouncing and emergent universe scenarios; suggests CMB polarization rotation as a potential observational probe of dark energy.
AI.conclusion: Quintom dark energy theory offers a viable framework to overcome the limitations of conventional dark energy models and provides observational avenues through CMB polarization measurements.

title: Inside-Out vs. Outside-In Quenching of MaNGA Galaxies: Dependence on Stellar Mass and Environment
summary: Galaxy quenching, the cessation of star formation, can proceed in spatially distinct ways, commonly described as inside-out or outside-in. However, the inferred quenching pattern depends strongly on how quenched or quenching regions are defined observationally. We utilize a sample of approximately 10,000 galaxies from the Mapping Nearby Galaxies at APO (MaNGA) DR17 survey to systematically compare four widely used diagnostics of star formation suppression: specific star formation rate (sSFR), the 4000 Å break (Dn4000), post-starburst (PSB), and low-ionization (nuclear) emission-line region (LI(N)ER) emission, to examine how tracer choice influences the inferred spatial quenching pattern. Using the non-parametric method developed by Lin et al. (2019), we classify galaxies into inside-out and outside-in quenching modes based on the location on the plane of the fraction of the quenched area (Fq) and the concentration of quenched area (Cq). We find that the sSFR criterion yields comparable proportions of galaxies classified as inside-out and outside-in, while Dn4000 and LI(N)ER diagnostics strongly favor inside-out patterns. Because PSB traces a distinct transitional phase, PSB-selected spaxels occupy a different region of the Fq-Cq plane. Across most diagnostics, the fraction of galaxies classified as inside-out increases with stellar mass, while outside-in patterns are more common in lower-mass systems, especially among satellites. In contrast, the dependence of quenching mode on halo mass is weaker and less consistent across diagnostics. These differences show that the tracers probe complementary stages and timescales of star-formation suppression, and together provide a more complete view of spatially resolved quenching.

AI.tldr: Using MaNGA DR17 data of ~10,000 galaxies, this paper systematically compares four diagnostics (sSFR, Dn4000, PSB, LI(N)ER) for classifying quenching patterns (inside-out vs. outside-in), finding that tracer choice strongly biases the inferred quenching mode: sSFR yields balanced classifications, Dn4000 and LI(N)ER favor inside-out, PSB traces a distinct transitional phase, and results depend on stellar mass and satellite status.
AI.motivation: The inferred spatial pattern of galaxy quenching (inside-out vs. outside-in) depends heavily on which observational diagnostic is used to define quenched regions, but a systematic comparison across multiple widely-used tracers has been lacking, motivating a comprehensive analysis to understand these biases.
AI.method: Analyzed ~10,000 MaNGA DR17 galaxies using four diagnostics: sSFR, Dn4000, PSB, and LI(N)ER. Used the non-parametric Fq-Cq plane method (Lin et al. 2019) to classify galaxies into inside-out and outside-in quenching modes, and compared classification outcomes across diagnostics as a function of stellar mass, halo mass, and satellite/central status.
AI.result: sSFR gives comparable fractions of inside-out and outside-in; Dn4000 and LI(N)ER strongly favor inside-out; PSB occupies a distinct region in Fq-Cq space. Inside-out fraction increases with stellar mass across most diagnostics; outside-in is more common in lower-mass and satellite galaxies. Halo mass dependence is weaker and less consistent.
AI.conclusion: Different quenching diagnostics probe complementary stages and timescales of star-formation suppression. No single tracer provides a complete picture; combining multiple diagnostics yields a more comprehensive view of spatially resolved quenching.

title: Optimal Transport Reconstruction of Biased Tracers in Primordial Non-Gaussian Fields
summary: Optimal transport provides an efficient method to infer the displacement of objects by mapping their initial positions to their present-day locations over cosmic time; equivalently, it enables the reconstruction of initial positions from measurements taken at later times. The method has been shown to be accurate even if positions for only a biased subset of the particles are measured, provided that the initial displacement field was Gaussian. The method does not rely on the assumption of a Gaussian displacement field, and thus may be extended to the reconstruction of non-Gaussian initial conditions. Here, we demonstrate how this is achieved for a class of "local" primordial non-Gaussian fields of current interest in cosmology. For these models, there is a distinctive signature in the large scale clustering of biased tracers which depends on the product of the primordial amplitude $f_{\rm NL}$ and the nature of the tracers $b_φ$. Our method exploits the fact that this signature is not present in the full field; it is only present in biased fields. Therefore, the mass that is not in the biased subset, what we call the "dust", also has a characteristic scale-dependence, albeit of a different amplitude. We show that the quality of the optimal transport reconstruction improves as the model for this dust becomes more realistic.

AI.tldr: Optimal transport can reconstruct initial cosmic positions from biased tracer data for non-Gaussian fields by modeling the "dust" (unbiased mass), with reconstruction quality improving as dust model becomes more realistic.
AI.motivation: To extend optimal transport-based reconstruction methods, previously limited to Gaussian initial conditions, to non-Gaussian primordial fields relevant to cosmology, specifically local-type primordial non-Gaussianity with parameter fNL.
AI.method: Exploits the fact that the scale-dependent bias signature (product fNL × bφ) appears only in biased tracer fields, not in the full field. Models the complementary "dust" component (unbiased mass) which has its own scale-dependent signature, and uses optimal transport to map initial to final positions.
AI.result: The quality of optimal transport reconstruction improves as the model for the dust component becomes more realistic.
AI.conclusion: Optimal transport reconstruction can be successfully extended to local-type primordial non-Gaussian fields by properly modeling the dust component, enabling inference of initial conditions from biased tracer data.

title: Multiwavelength study of the Carina--Sagittarius Arm. I.Astrometric and photometric search for new open clusters in the 320$^ \circ $ $\le$ l $\le$ 325$^ \circ $ region
summary: Our main goal is to determine whether the lower stellar density observed in the Carina-Sagittarius Arm region (320$^ \circ$ $\le$ l $\le$ 325$^ \circ$, $|b| \le$ $1^ \circ$) is an intrinsic structural feature of the spiral arm or a consequence of high interstellar reddening and extinction along the line of sight. We performed a systematic search for new open clusters using the HDBSCAN algorithm on Gaia DR3 astrometric data. The physical reality of the candidates was validated through a multiwavelength analysis, integrating Gaia photometry with NIR of the 2MASS catalog, MIR photometric information of the WISE catalog to identify young stellar objects (YSOs), and the radio continuum emission at 843 MHz with SUMSS survey to identify and associated interstellar material. We report the discovery of five new open clusters, the ESFERA sample. Our analysis reveals four young systems (10-50 Myr), with ESFERA 3 hosting YSOs, while ESFERA 5 is identified as a 2 Gyr old cluster. Although the region lacks massive star-forming complexes, these clusters trace active, despite the fact that lower-efficiency, star formation within the region. Our results suggest that this region represents an intrinsic star-formation "valley" or low-density node (the "string" in a "beads on a string" morphology) rather than an effect of extinction. The discovery of these clusters demonstrates that while the local surface density is below the critical threshold for massive complexes, star formation persists in isolated, small-scale pockets throughout the arm.

AI.tldr: Using HDBSCAN on Gaia DR3 data, we discovered five new open clusters (ESFERA sample) in the Carina-Sagittarius Arm region (l=320°–325°). Multiwavelength validation shows four young (10–50 Myr) clusters and one old (2 Gyr) cluster. The region's low stellar density is an intrinsic structural feature—a star-formation "valley" or low-density node—not an extinction effect, indicating star formation persists in isolated pockets despite sub-critical surface density for massive complexes.
AI.motivation: To determine whether the low stellar density in the Carina-Sagittarius Arm region (l=320°–325°) is an intrinsic structural feature of the spiral arm or caused by high interstellar reddening/extinction.
AI.method: Systematic search for new open clusters using HDBSCAN on Gaia DR3 astrometric data, validated via multiwavelength analysis including Gaia photometry, 2MASS NIR, WISE MIR (for YSOs), and SUMSS 843 MHz radio continuum.
AI.result: Discovery of five new open clusters (ESFERA sample): four young (10–50 Myr) including ESFERA 3 with YSOs, and one old (2 Gyr, ESFERA 5). The region lacks massive star-forming complexes but shows active, low-efficiency star formation.
AI.conclusion: The region is an intrinsic star-formation "valley" or low-density node ("string" in "beads on a string" morphology) rather than an extinction effect. Star formation persists in isolated, small-scale pockets despite sub-critical local surface density for massive complexes.

title: Primordial black holes spin from cosmological first-order phase transitions
summary: The stochastic bubble nucleation during cosmological first-order phase transitions leads to variations in the phase transition initiation times across different Hubble volumes, thereby generating non-Gaussian density perturbations in regions with delayed transitions. Based on the accumulation mechanism and the false vacuum island model . This paper investigates the spin angular momentum of primordial black holes formed from nonspherical collapse. By introducing the nucleation history integration method, without assuming a Gaussian distribution, we calculate the expectation values and variances of the semi-axis lengths of overdense ellipsoidal regions, combined with the statistical properties of the velocity shear tensor, we derive the quantitative relationship between the Kerr parameter $a_*$ describing black hole spin and the phase transition parameters , latent heat strength $α$ and phase transition rate $β$. The study finds that the Kerr parameter increases with $α$ and decreases with $β$; estimate the typical the magnitude of $a_*$ can reach $10^{-3}$, which is significantly higher than that of primordial black holes formed in the radiation-dominated era under peak theory, but still lower than that in a matter-dominated era.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the spin angular momentum of primordial black holes formed from nonspherical collapse during cosmological first-order phase transitions. Using a nucleation history integration method, the authors derive the relationship between the Kerr parameter a_* (black hole spin) and phase transition parameters α (latent heat strength) and β (phase transition rate). They find that a_* increases with α and decreases with β, with typical magnitude around 10^{-3}, higher than radiation-dominated era PBHs but lower than matter-dominated era PBHs.
AI.motivation: To understand how stochastic bubble nucleation during first-order phase transitions generates non-Gaussian density perturbations, and to quantify the spin angular momentum of primordial black holes formed from nonspherical collapse in such scenarios.
AI.method: The paper employs a nucleation history integration method without assuming Gaussian distributions, calculates expectation values and variances of semi-axis lengths of overdense ellipsoidal regions, and combines these with statistical properties of the velocity shear tensor to derive a quantitative relationship between the Kerr parameter a_* and phase transition parameters.
AI.result: The Kerr parameter a_* increases with latent heat strength α and decreases with phase transition rate β. The typical magnitude of a_* is approximately 10^{-3}, which is significantly higher than PBHs formed in the radiation-dominated era (under peak theory) but lower than those formed in a matter-dominated era.
AI.conclusion: The spin of PBHs from first-order phase transitions is non-negligible and depends predictably on the phase transition parameters, offering potential observational signatures for distinguishing formation scenarios.

title: The Information Content of Quasar Variability Light Curves: How Well Can we Infer Stochastic Model Parameters?
summary: Quasar variability, driven by multi-scale physical processing within a relativistic accretion disk, is commonly modelled with stochastic time series models. The simplest of these is the Damped Random Walk (DRW), also known as the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) process. Here, we demonstrate that, when fitting such a model to quasar light curve data, the mean of the light curve, $μ$, should not be fixed (which is the typical approach), as this leads to overconfident inferences about the variability timescale $τ$, with substantially underestimated uncertainties. However, the short term volatility parameter $η$ is typically very well constrained from short light curves. Through simulations, we compute information theoretic quantities such as the conditional entropy and the mutual information, confirming that light curves provide much more information about $η$ than about $τ$. As a result, we recommend that future quasar variability studies focus on $η$ rather than $τ$. To demonstrate this approach, we fit a hierarchical Bayesian regression model for $η$ as a function of bolometric luminosity and rest wavelength to a dataset of 570 light curves measured over decades. We perform the fit using a likelihood function that uses the light curves directly, rather than using intermediate $η$ values from individual light curve fits. We find that volatility decreases as a function of both bolometric luminosity and rest wavelength. The volatility also decreases more steeply with redshift than time dilation alone would suggest, pointing to an increase in intrinsic volatility as quasars evolve over cosmic time.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that fixing the mean when fitting Damped Random Walk models to quasar light curves leads to overconfident estimates of the variability timescale τ, and recommends focusing on the short-term volatility parameter η instead, which is better constrained. A hierarchical Bayesian model reveals that η decreases with bolometric luminosity, rest wavelength, and evolves with redshift beyond time dilation.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that common practice of fixing the mean μ in DRW/OU process fits to quasar light curves causes underestimated uncertainties for the variability timescale τ, and to advocate shifting focus to the better-constrained volatility parameter η.
AI.method: Simulations compute conditional entropy and mutual information to quantify information content about τ vs η. A hierarchical Bayesian regression model for η (function of bolometric luminosity and rest wavelength) is fit using a likelihood function applied directly to 570 light curves, avoiding intermediate η estimates from individual fits.
AI.result: η is much better constrained than τ; fixing μ overconfidently narrows τ uncertainties. Volatility η decreases with both bolometric luminosity and rest wavelength, and decreases more steeply with redshift than time dilation alone predicts, indicating intrinsic evolution of quasar variability over cosmic time.
AI.conclusion: Future quasar variability studies should prioritize η over τ. The hierarchical Bayesian approach yields robust population-level constraints, revealing luminosity, wavelength, and redshift dependencies of quasar volatility.

title: CSST large-scale structure analysis pipeline: IV. Cosmic Voids Identified from Galaxy Group Samples as Probes of the Large-scale Structure
summary: Because groups are directly associated with halos, they allow for considerably simpler theoretical modeling than approaches based on individual galaxies. We therefore propose to use voids identified in galaxy group catalogs, referred to as group-voids, to investigate the cosmic large-scale structure (LSS). Using the reference mock galaxy redshift survey (MGRS) designed for the Chinese Space-station Survey Telescope (CSST), we build two galaxy group catalogs representing ideal and conservative scenarios, derived from galaxy samples with 100\% and roughly 30\% spectroscopic redshift completeness, respectively. We then identify voids in these two mock group catalogs, as well as in the underlying halo catalog, and measure two void statistics, the void size function (VSF) and the void density profile, within five redshift intervals spanning $z=0$ to $1.0$. We compare the statistics obtained from two kinds of voids: those defined by galaxy groups (group-voids) and those defined by dark matter halos (halo-voids). In the void-finding process, we adopt the brightest central galaxy (BCG) as the group center to improve the accuracy of the inferred void centers. Our analysis shows that void statistics derived from group-voids with spectroscopic redshift completeness of at least 40\% can faithfully reproduce the corresponding statistics from halo-voids. Even when the redshift completeness of galaxies falls to as low as 30\%, we can still reliably describe group-voids via halo-voids by incorporating a redshift error term. This indicates that group-voids are a promising tool for probing LSS and offer a valuable complement to standard void studies, which is especially advantageous for emulator-based methods.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using voids identified in galaxy group catalogs (group-voids) as an alternative to halo-based voids for studying large-scale structure. Using CSST mock data, they show that group-voids can faithfully reproduce halo-void statistics even with spectroscopic redshift completeness as low as 30%, making them a promising tool for cosmological analysis.
AI.motivation: Groups are directly associated with halos, enabling simpler theoretical modeling than individual galaxy-based approaches. The authors aim to validate group-voids as reliable tracers of cosmic large-scale structure that can work with lower spectroscopic completeness.
AI.method: Using CSST reference mock galaxy redshift surveys, two group catalogs were built (ideal: 100% completeness; conservative: ~30% completeness). Voids were identified in both group and halo catalogs across five redshift bins (z=0 to 1.0). Void size function and void density profiles were measured using BCG as group center. Group-voids were compared to halo-voids with and without redshift error corrections.
AI.result: Group-voids with ≥40% spectroscopic completeness faithfully reproduce halo-void statistics. Even at 30% completeness, group-void statistics can be reliably matched to halo-voids after incorporating a redshift error term. Void statistics from group-voids with BCG centers show good consistency with halo-void results.
AI.conclusion: Group-voids are a promising alternative to halo-voids for studying large-scale structure, particularly advantageous for emulator-based methods, as they maintain fidelity even with reduced spectroscopic completeness.

title: Morphology of Optical Changing-Look AGN-host Galaxies: Evidence for an Important Role of Mergers
summary: Optical changing-look active galactic nuclei (CL-AGNs) are characterized by the (dis)appearance of broad emission lines on unexpectedly short timescales. However, the underlying mechanisms and their potential connection to host-galaxy properties are still unclear. In this work, we present an analysis of the morphology for 63 low-redshift CL-AGNs (z < 0.15) selected from the largest CL-AGN catalog (Guo et al. 2025) to date, using images from DESI DR10 and employing both non-parametric methods and visual inspection. We find that CL-AGN hosts exhibit a concentration like late-type spirals, asymmetry like early-type spirals, and smoothness like ellipticals. This is confirmed by their Gini-M20 coefficients, suggesting weak/modest disturbances. Based upon our visual inspection, we further identify that 18 (29%) out of 63 sources are mergers, among which ~56% (10/18) show shell features. Compared to different non-CL-AGN samples, CL-AGN hosts have a higher (~2\times) possibility of being merging systems. Our results indicate that mergers/interactions may play an important role in driving the changing-look behavior.

AI.tldr: Analysis of 63 low-redshift CL-AGNs reveals their host galaxies exhibit mixed morphological properties (concentrated like late-type spirals, asymmetric like early-type spirals, smooth like ellipticals) with 29% being merging systems (~2× higher than non-CL-AGN controls), suggesting mergers/interactions play an important role in driving changing-look behavior.
AI.motivation: The underlying mechanisms driving the (dis)appearance of broad emission lines in CL-AGNs and their potential connection to host-galaxy properties remain unclear.
AI.method: Morphological analysis of 63 low-redshift CL-AGNs (z<0.15) from Guo et al. (2025) catalog using DESI DR10 images, employing non-parametric methods (concentration, asymmetry, smoothness, Gini-M20) and visual inspection.
AI.result: CL-AGN hosts show concentration like late-type spirals, asymmetry like early-type spirals, and smoothness like ellipticals; Gini-M20 indicates weak/modest disturbances. 29% (18/63) are mergers, ~56% of which show shell features. CL-AGN hosts have ~2× higher merger fraction than non-CL-AGN samples.
AI.conclusion: Mergers/interactions may play an important role in driving the changing-look behavior in AGNs.

title: Redshift Duality with Pantheon+SH0ES in a Planck-anchored Flat $Λ$CDM Framework: Implications for Hubble Tension and Observational Inference
comment: Author version comprising 31 pages and 5 figures. Compiled in the MNRAS LaTeX style. Compared with the Advance Access version, this version includes accessibility-related updates to figure captions, updated affiliation and acknowledgements, revised citation labels, and corrected mathematical notation
summary: We test an operationally defined redshift duality in which the observed redshift comprises the standard metric-expansion component together with an additional line-of-sight quantum contribution arising from the cumulative conversion of photon energy into effective mass as a function of path length and frequency. Fitting this hybrid model to the Pantheon+SH0ES compilation, we find that the metric-expansion Hubble constant, $H_Λ$, is recovered to a value consistent with the Planck baseline of $67.4~\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$ within $\lesssim 0.33σ$. Redshift-binned analyses show that while the flat Lambda cold dark matter ($Λ$CDM) model produces an apparent drift in the inferred Hubble parameter across the Hubble flow, the hybrid model restores the constancy of $H_Λ$ across redshift bins. The correctional trends of cosmological physical quantities re-inferred under this framework further indicate the potential to alleviate anomalies associated with high-redshift galaxies. These results suggest that redshift duality warrants further consideration in observational processing and inference, while preserving consistency with a Planck-anchored flat $Λ$CDM baseline.

AI.tldr: The paper tests a redshift duality model combining standard metric expansion with a quantum contribution from photon-to-mass conversion. Fitting to Pantheon+SH0ES data yields a Hubble constant consistent with Planck's $67.4~\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$ (within $0.33σ$). The hybrid model restores constancy of $H_Λ$ across redshift bins, unlike flat $Λ$CDM, and may alleviate high-redshift galaxy anomalies.
AI.motivation: To resolve tensions (e.g., Hubble constant discrepancy) by testing an operationally defined redshift duality where observed redshift includes both metric-expansion and a quantum line-of-sight component from photon energy converting to effective mass along the path.
AI.method: The hybrid redshift model (metric expansion + quantum contribution) is fitted to the Pantheon+SH0ES supernova compilation. Redshift-binned analyses compare the constancy of the inferred Hubble parameter between flat $Λ$CDM and the hybrid model.
AI.result: The hybrid model recovers $H_Λ = 67.4~\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$ (Planck value) within $<0.33σ$. Unlike $Λ$CDM, which shows drift in $H(z)$ across bins, the hybrid model restores constancy of $H_Λ$ and suggests corrections that may alleviate high-redshift galaxy anomalies.
AI.conclusion: Redshift duality warrants further consideration in observational processing and inference, as it preserves consistency with a Planck-anchored flat $Λ$CDM baseline while resolving certain cosmological tensions.

title: Signatures of Accreting Black Holes in Line Intensity Mapping
summary: Line-intensity mapping (LIM) has attracted growing attention as a powerful technique for probing the large-scale distribution of galaxies and the cosmic history of star formation through unresolved line emission. Existing LIM models for galaxy-associated lines, such as H$α$, often assume that the dominant contribution to observed emission arises from star-forming activity, while the role of accreting black holes (BHs) remains largely unexplored. In this study, we use the IllustrisTNG cosmological hydrodynamical simulation to construct mock intensity maps of H$α$ and He II, including contributions from both star formation and BH accretion. We show that the BH contribution to the mean intensity is significant, reaching $\sim$40--60 per cent for H$α$ and $\sim$60--80 per cent for He II around cosmic noon. Owing to the large luminosity weight of rare, bright sources, BH-powered emission dominates the shot-noise component of the power spectrum and significantly boosts the small-scale clustering amplitude, particularly for He II. We assess the implications for forthcoming LIM surveys and show that SPHEREx can probe the BH-influenced bright end of the H$α$ voxel intensity distribution (VID) at $z\lesssim4$, and a CDIM-like experiment can further access the BH-dominated regime of He II. Our results demonstrate that accreting BHs represent an essential component of LIM signals, which was previously underappreciated. We thus conclude that accurately modeling the BH contribution is crucial for a physically complete interpretation of future LIM observations.

AI.tldr: Using IllustrisTNG simulations, this study shows that accreting black holes contribute significantly (~40-80%) to Hα and He II line-intensity mapping signals at cosmic noon, dominating shot noise and small-scale clustering, with implications for SPHEREx and CDIM surveys.
AI.motivation: Existing LIM models for galaxy-associated lines (e.g., Hα) typically attribute observed emission solely to star formation, neglecting the potentially important role of accreting black holes.
