AI.method: The study uses the IllustrisTNG cosmological hydrodynamical simulation to construct mock intensity maps of Hα and He II, incorporating contributions from both star formation and BH accretion.
AI.result: BH contribution to mean intensity reaches ~40-60% for Hα and ~60-80% for He II at cosmic noon. BH-powered emission dominates the shot-noise component and boosts small-scale clustering, especially for He II. SPHEREx can probe the BH-influenced bright end of Hα VID at z≲4; a CDIM-like experiment can access the BH-dominated regime of He II.
AI.conclusion: Accreting BHs are an essential, previously underappreciated component of LIM signals; accurate BH modeling is crucial for physically complete interpretation of future LIM observations.

title: JWST's Little Red Dots as collapsed Supermassive Dark Stars
summary: The nature of the ``Little Red Dots'' (LRDs) is one of the most profound mysteries posed by the JWST data. One promising class of models that can reproduce the observed LRDs spectra and morphology are quasi-stars: massive envelopes surrounding accreting black holes formed via the collapse of supermassive stars (SMSs). However, the canonical SMS pathway relies on a highly restricted set of environmental and structural conditions: strong Lyman--Werner (LW) backgrounds to suppress H$_2$ cooling, high and sustained gas inflow rates to enforce entropy stratified envelopes, and assume non-zero rotational support in order to prevent GR instability collapse before $\sim 10^6 M_{\odot}$. Here we show that supermassive dark stars (SMDSs), powered by dark matter (DM) annihilation rather than nuclear burning, naturally satisfy the key structural and energetic requirements for quasi-star (QS) formation while relaxing {\it all} of those restrictive conditions listed above. Moreover, quasi-stars formed through the SMDS pathway are born with prompt BH masses ($\gtrsim 10\%$) of the progenitor mass. They therefore enter directly into a late-stage quasi-star regime; subsequently the envelope expands and cools until its photosphere reaches the zero-metallicity opacity limit $(T_{\rm eff}\sim3000$-$6000\,{\rm K}$). Those cool, optically thick, unresolved photospheres can reproduce key features of many JWST LRDs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes that supermassive dark stars (SMDSs), powered by dark matter annihilation, can naturally evolve into quasi-stars that explain the observed properties of JWST's "Little Red Dots" (LRDs), overcoming the restrictive conditions required by canonical supermassive star models.
AI.motivation: To explain the nature of JWST's "Little Red Dots" (LRDs) — a major mystery — by identifying a viable formation pathway for quasi-stars that avoids the highly restrictive environmental, structural, and rotational conditions required by the canonical supermassive star model.
AI.method: The authors compare the canonical supermassive star (SMS) pathway (requiring strong Lyman-Werner backgrounds, high sustained inflow rates, and rotational support) with the supermassive dark star (SMDS) pathway (powered by dark matter annihilation), showing that SMDSs naturally meet the structural and energetic prerequisites for quasi-star formation without those restrictive conditions.
AI.result: SMDS-formed quasi-stars have prompt black hole masses ≥10% of the progenitor mass, directly enter a late-stage quasi-star regime, and produce cool (Teff ~3000–6000 K), optically thick, unresolved photospheres that can reproduce key features of many JWST LRDs.
AI.conclusion: The SMDS pathway offers a viable and less restrictive alternative to the canonical SMS model for forming quasi-stars, naturally explaining the observed spectra and morphology of JWST's Little Red Dots.

title: Magneto-Gravitational Regulated Streamer Accretion onto a Class 0 Protostellar System
comment: 27 pages, 7 figures and 2 tables, published on Science Advances (22nd May 2026)
summary: How do magnetic fields shape the way young stars gather gas from their birth clouds? Using high-resolution Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array observations of a young triple protostellar system HOPS-182, we identify an elongated stream of gas, or accretion streamer, that extends over several thousand astronomical units (1 astronomical unit is the Earth-Sun distance) and carries a substantial flow of material toward the system. The gas speeds along this filament increase toward the star in a way consistent with gravitational free-fall, while the streamer's shape closely follows the magnetic field threading the region. By comparing the strengths of gravity and magnetic tension and measuring how the gas rotates compared with the local magnetic field, we show that the field is strong enough to help confine and guide the infalling gas and efficiently remove angular momentum. These results suggest that a substantial fraction of the material falling onto young protostellar systems can be funneled through elongated, magnetically structured accretion streamers.

AI.tldr: Using ALMA observations of the HOPS-182 triple protostellar system, we identify a magnetically guided accretion streamer extending thousands of AU, where gas follows free-fall velocities and magnetic fields help confine and guide infalling material while removing angular momentum.
AI.motivation: To understand how magnetic fields influence the gas accretion process onto young protostellar systems, specifically whether and how they shape the infall pathways.
AI.method: High-resolution ALMA observations of the HOPS-182 triple protostellar system, measuring gas kinematics (velocities), streamer morphology, magnetic field alignment, and comparing gravitational vs. magnetic tension forces.
AI.result: An elongated accretion streamer extending over several thousand AU was identified, with gas speeds increasing inward consistent with free-fall. The streamer aligns closely with the local magnetic field, and magnetic tension is strong enough to confine, guide, and remove angular momentum from the infalling gas.
AI.conclusion: Magnetic fields play a key role in structuring accretion onto young stars, funneling a substantial fraction of infalling material through elongated, magnetically guided accretion streamers.

title: Accurate inner stellar density slopes from projected surface densities in galaxies
comment: Accepted for publication in ApJ. The main results are in Eqs. (9) and (20)
summary: The inner slope of the three-dimensional stellar density in dwarf galaxies (rho'[0]) is a sensitive probe of possible departures from the collisionless cold dark matter (CDM) paradigm, since cored stellar distributions (rho'[0]=0) cannot easily reside within the cuspy potentials CDM predicts for low-mass systems. Photometry alone offers an observationally inexpensive way to constrain rho'(0), making this approach particularly attractive for the faint galaxies most relevant to dark matter (DM) studies. Inferring volume densities, however, requires deprojecting the observed stellar surface density, Sigma(R), a procedure that is notoriously ambiguous in the presence of noise. To avoid explicit deprojection, we derive an expression (Eq.~[9]]) to obtain rho'(0) directly from the radial derivatives of Sigma(R), assuming spherical symmetry and smooth finite density profiles. All projected profiles are shown to have the same central functional form, independent of the underlying volume density (Eq.~[20]). As a result, the derivatives of Sigma(R) can be extrapolated to the center using constraints from larger radii, which in turn yields rho'(0). As an illustration, we apply the method to six ultra-faint dwarf (UFD) galaxies, finding that all of them have a surface density with the same shape, from which the presence of stellar cores is inferred (rho'[0] simeq 0). The technique also has the ability to diagnose rho'[0]>0, corresponding to galaxies with a central stellar mass deficit potentially linked to black-hole scouring, MONDian dynamics, or deviations from CDM.

AI.tldr: The paper derives a method to directly infer the central stellar density slope rho'(0) in dwarf galaxies from projected surface brightness profiles, avoiding ambiguous deprojection. Applied to six ultra-faint dwarfs, all show cored stellar distributions (rho'[0] ≈ 0), consistent with cored potentials rather than cuspy CDM predictions.
AI.motivation: The inner slope of the 3D stellar density in dwarf galaxies (rho'[0]) is a sensitive probe of departures from collisionless CDM, since cored stellar distributions (rho'[0]=0) cannot easily reside within the cuspy CDM potentials predicted for low-mass systems. Photometry offers an observationally inexpensive way to constrain this, especially for faint galaxies relevant to DM studies.
AI.method: The authors derive an expression (Eq. 9) to obtain rho'(0) directly from radial derivatives of the observed surface density Sigma(R), assuming spherical symmetry and smooth finite density profiles, thus avoiding explicit deprojection. They show all projected profiles share the same central functional form (Eq. 20), allowing extrapolation of Sigma(R) derivatives from larger radii to infer rho'(0).
AI.result: Applied to six ultra-faint dwarf (UFD) galaxies, all exhibit surface densities with the same shape, from which stellar cores are inferred (rho'[0] ≈ 0). The technique can also diagnose rho'(0) > 0, indicating central stellar mass deficits potentially linked to black-hole scouring, MONDian dynamics, or deviations from CDM.
AI.conclusion: The method provides a robust, deprojection-free way to constrain central stellar density slopes in dwarf galaxies. The finding of cored stellar profiles in all six UFDs supports the presence of cored underlying potentials, challenging the cuspy CDM prediction for low-mass systems.

title: Mergers Matter: Gravothermal Collapse in Dwarf Halos with Self-Interacting Dark Matter
summary: Self-Interacting Dark Matter (SIDM) models with large cross sections at relative velocities below $\sim100\,{\rm km \, s}^{-1}$ can be tested with dwarf galaxy observations. We analyze six dark-matter-only zoom-in $\sim10^{10}\,{\rm M}_\odot$ halos with diverse assembly histories, adopting a cross section over mass of $σ/m = 70\,cm^2 \, g^{-1}$. We find that mergers inject orbital kinetic energy into the halo, altering the heat transport and the gravothermal evolution of the core. Three of the six halos -- those with the most quiescent merger histories -- show clear signs of core collapse in these simulations. Halos with sustained mergers do not collapse. Furthermore, merger-induced heat transport drives two non-collapsing halos to central densities well below the predictions of the gravothermal fluid model. These findings suggest a novel mechanism for producing dark-matter-deficient galaxies and expanding the diversity of rotation curves beyond what halo concentration alone predicts. Merger histories are thus essential for understanding central density distributions of dwarf galaxy halos in SIDM.

AI.tldr: SIDM simulations show that merger history critically determines whether dwarf galaxy halos undergo core collapse or become dark-matter-deficient, with quiescent halos collapsing and actively merging halos exhibiting suppressed central densities.
AI.motivation: To test SIDM models with large cross sections at low relative velocities using dwarf galaxy observations, and understand how merger histories affect gravothermal evolution of halo cores.
AI.method: Six dark-matter-only zoom-in simulations of ~10^10 M⊙ halos with diverse assembly histories, adopting σ/m = 70 cm² g⁻¹, analyzing the impact of mergers on heat transport and core evolution.
AI.result: Three quiescent-merger halos undergo core collapse; halos with sustained mergers do not collapse. Merger-induced heat transport drives two non-collapsing halos to central densities below gravothermal fluid model predictions, suggesting a mechanism for dark-matter-deficient galaxies.
AI.conclusion: Merger histories are essential for understanding central density distributions of dwarf galaxy halos in SIDM, and can produce greater diversity in rotation curves than predicted by concentration alone.

title: Radio Continuum Emission from Evolving Star-Forming Galaxies -- I. Correlations Involving the Total Synchrotron Luminosity
comment: Main text 35 pages, 30 figures, and 8 tables. Submitted to ApJ. Comments welcome!
summary: Synchrotron radiation dominates the continuum emission of star-forming galaxies in the frequency range from a few $\rm MHz$ to about $30\,\rm{GHz}$. We model the total synchrotron emission of a large population of evolving star-forming galaxies using the semi-analytic galaxy formation model GALFORM combined with the dynamo simulation code MAGNETIZER. Assuming local energy equipartition between cosmic rays and magnetic fields, we calculate the specific synchrotron luminosity $L_ν$ for each simulated galaxy at various frequencies and find strong positive correlations between $L_ν$ and both the star formation rate ($\rm SFR$) and characteristic galaxy rotation speed $V_{\rm rot}$ for redshifts up to $z\simeq 3$. At low redshifts, the turbulent magnetic field is found to dominate in the synchrotron luminosity, but the contribution of the large-scale magnetic field increases with redshift and becomes important for $z\gtrsim 1$. The correlation between $L_ν$ and $\rm SFR$ arises from the tight correlation between the disc gas mass $M_{\rm gas}$ and $\rm SFR$, and the correlation between $L_ν$ and $V_{\rm rot}$ is additionally a consequence of the stellar mass Tully--Fisher relation for main-sequence galaxies. At low redshifts, the model predictions and observational data compiled for this work show remarkable agreement, but a discrepancy arises at higher redshifts, where modelled $\rm SFR$ values are systematically smaller than those previously inferred from observations. These theoretical models will aid the interpretation of next-generation radio surveys with the Square Kilometre Array and other telescopes.

AI.tldr: This paper uses the GALFORM semi-analytic model and MAGNETIZER dynamo code to model synchrotron emission from star-forming galaxies, finding strong correlations between synchrotron luminosity, star formation rate, and rotation speed up to z~3. The turbulent magnetic field dominates at low redshifts while the large-scale field becomes important at z>1. Model predictions agree with observations at low redshifts but show discrepancies at higher redshifts, with implications for upcoming radio surveys like the Square Kilometre Array.
AI.motivation: To model the synchrotron emission from evolving star-forming galaxies across cosmic time, incorporating magnetic field generation via the dynamo process, and to provide theoretical predictions for interpreting next-generation radio surveys such as the Square Kilometre Array.
AI.method: The authors combine the semi-analytic galaxy formation model GALFORM with the dynamo simulation code MAGNETIZER, assuming local energy equipartition between cosmic rays and magnetic fields, to calculate the specific synchrotron luminosity for each simulated galaxy at various frequencies.
AI.result: Strong positive correlations are found between synchrotron luminosity L_ν and both star formation rate (SFR) and characteristic rotation speed V_rot up to z~3. The turbulent magnetic field dominates at low redshifts, but the large-scale field contribution increases with redshift and becomes important for z>1. Model predictions agree with observations at low redshifts, but at higher redshifts the modelled SFR values are systematically lower than previously inferred from observations.
AI.conclusion: The models provide a framework for interpreting next-generation radio surveys, though discrepancies at high redshift suggest the need for refinements. The correlations originate from the M_gas-SFR relation and the stellar mass Tully-Fisher relation for main-sequence galaxies.

title: A study of the Physical Properties and Star Formation Activity of a Large Sample of Molecular Clouds: I Distances
comment: 18 pages, 14 figures, 2 tables, accepted by ApJS
summary: Accurate distances to molecular clouds are crucial for determining their physical properties, understanding star formation, and tracing Galactic spiral structure. A number of 103,517 molecular clouds has been identified by the DBSCAN algorithm in the MWISP Phase I CO survey (l = 9.75-229.75 deg, |b| <= 5.25 deg), most of which lack reliable distances. In this work, we propose three independent methods, all of which match the molecular cloud's velocity-integrated intensity maps of 12CO lines from the MWISP with the three-dimensional dust extinction maps derived from Gaia, Pan-STARRS 1, and 2MASS, to determine molecular cloud distances. We present a catalog of 1,573 molecular clouds with robust distances ranging from approximately 150 pc to 3000 pc, 90 percent of which are measured for the first time, with typical statistical and systematic uncertainties of approximately 20% and 10%, respectively. We also derive their physical properties, such as their mass and sizes. This publicly available catalog of molecular clouds with distances provides a foundation for testing molecular cloud scaling relations and probing how cloud conditions influence star formation across diverse Galactic environments.

AI.tldr: Present a catalog of 1,573 molecular clouds with robust distances (0.15-3 kpc) derived by matching MWISP CO data with 3D dust extinction maps from Gaia, Pan-STARRS 1, and 2MASS, using three independent methods.
AI.motivation: Accurate distances to molecular clouds are essential for determining physical properties, understanding star formation, and tracing Galactic spiral structure, yet most of the 103,517 clouds identified by MWISP Phase I CO survey lack reliable distances.
AI.method: Three independent methods that match velocity-integrated intensity maps of 12CO lines from MWISP with 3D dust extinction maps from Gaia, Pan-STARRS 1, and 2MASS to determine distances.
AI.result: Catalog of 1,573 molecular clouds with distances ~150 pc to 3000 pc; 90% measured for the first time; typical statistical uncertainty ~20%, systematic uncertainty ~10%.
AI.conclusion: This publicly available catalog provides a foundation for testing molecular cloud scaling relations and probing how cloud conditions influence star formation across diverse Galactic environments.

title: Hierarchical assembly in action: a galaxy tail from a disrupting group in the Virgo cluster outskirts
comment: 9 figures, 14 pages, accepted for publication at A&A
summary: Group environments are thought to play a key role in shaping galaxy evolution prior to cluster accretion. However, direct observational evidence linking group--cluster interactions to the transformation of low-mass galaxies remains scarce. We reexamine the nature and origin of the W cloud, located in the southern outskirts of the Virgo cluster, to better understand the dynamical processes driving group accretion and galaxy transformation during cluster assembly. Using the spatial distribution, kinematics, and stellar population properties of galaxies in the W cloud and its surroundings, we characterize the three-dimensional structure and dynamical state of the system. We show that the W cloud is not a large-scale filament seen in projection, but is instead dominated by a compact galaxy group (the W group) currently interacting with Virgo. We also identify a previously unknown, dynamically coherent tail of galaxies (the W tail) connecting the W group to the cluster. The tail exhibits a continuous sequence in velocity, velocity dispersion, and three-dimensional distance. Its low-velocity component is already gravitationally bound to Virgo, whereas higher-velocity galaxies remain associated with the W group and are still infalling. The W tail forms a planar structure aligned with the orbital geometry of the W group, strongly supporting a tidal origin. The stellar masses and colours of its members indicate that the stripped population is dominated by low-mass, star-forming dwarf galaxies that remain in the blue cloud. The W group--W tail system provides a well-resolved example of an ongoing group--cluster interaction, illustrating how low-density groups can deliver largely unprocessed dwarf galaxies into clusters. This system provides important observational constraints on the hierarchical assembly of galaxy clusters and the buildup of their dwarf galaxy populations.

AI.tldr: The W cloud in the Virgo cluster outskirts is actually a compact group (the W group) interacting with the cluster, producing a tidal tail (the W tail) of low-mass, star-forming dwarf galaxies being stripped during infall. This provides a clear observational example of hierarchical group accretion delivering unprocessed dwarf galaxies into clusters.
AI.motivation: To understand how group environments drive galaxy evolution prior to cluster accretion, by reexamining the nature and origin of the W cloud in the Virgo cluster's southern outskirts.
AI.method: Analysis of spatial distribution, kinematics, and stellar population properties of galaxies in the W cloud and its surroundings to characterize the 3D structure and dynamical state of the system.
AI.result: The W cloud is a compact group (W group) interacting with Virgo, with a dynamically coherent tidal tail (W tail) connecting the group to the cluster. The tail shows a continuous velocity sequence; low-velocity galaxies are bound to Virgo while high-velocity ones remain infalling with the group. The tail is planar and aligned with the group's orbital geometry. Stripped galaxies are low-mass, star-forming dwarfs still in the blue cloud.
AI.conclusion: The W group–W tail system is a well-resolved example of ongoing group–cluster interaction, showing how low-density groups deliver largely unprocessed dwarf galaxies into clusters, providing observational constraints on hierarchical cluster assembly and dwarf galaxy population buildup.

title: The magnetic field of the Milky Way: an observational perspective
comment: Invited review article for The Astronomy and Astrophysics Review. Submitted, comments welcome
summary:
Magnetic fields are an important and enigmatic component of the Milky Way's ecosystem. Mostly frozen into interstellar plasma, they play key roles in (turbulent) gas dynamics, star formation, energy household, evolution of interstellar objects, and cosmic-ray propagation. This paper reviews recent progress on measuring and characterizing these Galactic magnetic fields, limited to the larger-scale fields in mostly diffuse media, and to an observational perspective.
  On Galaxy-wide scales, the magnetic field roughly follows the spiral arms in the Galactic disk, and includes an additional component perpendicular to the disk away from the Galactic plane. The field configuration is different in the Galactic disk and the Galactic gaseous halo, qualitatively consistent with different dominating dynamo modes. Deviations from this idealized model are ubiquitously observed and include anomalously high Faraday rotation, variable magnetic field orientations and field reversals on kiloparsec scales.
  On smaller scales, the magnetic field is turbulent, anisotropic and intermittent. Much used descriptions of the turbulent magnetic field such as power laws and Gaussianity are being replaced by higher-order statistics that better capture the complexities of the field. Magnetic field orientations and possibly strength are correlated with both cold and warm components of the multi-phase interstellar gas, and with the interstellar dust distribution.
  The near future will bring a large increase in observational data in rotation measure grids, Faraday Tomography data and measurements of interstellar polarization of optical starlight, promising exciting developments in characterizing and understanding magnetic fields in the Milky Way in the next few years.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews recent observational progress on measuring and characterizing Milky Way magnetic fields on large scales in diffuse media, covering Galaxy-wide field structure, turbulent small-scale fields, and upcoming observational advances.
AI.motivation: Magnetic fields are a crucial yet poorly understood component of the Milky Way, influencing gas dynamics, star formation, energy balance, interstellar object evolution, and cosmic-ray propagation; the paper aims to synthesize recent observational progress on characterizing these fields.
AI.method: The paper is a review limited to an observational perspective on larger-scale magnetic fields in mostly diffuse media, summarizing recent findings from measurements such as Faraday rotation, Faraday Tomography, and interstellar polarization of optical starlight.
AI.result: On Galaxy-wide scales, the magnetic field roughly follows spiral arms in the disk with a perpendicular component away from the plane; field configuration differs between disk and gaseous halo, consistent with different dynamo modes, with observed deviations including anomalous Faraday rotation, variable field orientations, and kiloparsec-scale field reversals. On smaller scales, the field is turbulent, anisotropic, and intermittent, with higher-order statistics replacing power-law and Gaussian descriptions.
AI.conclusion: The near future will bring a large increase in rotation measure grids, Faraday Tomography data, and interstellar polarization measurements, promising exciting progress in characterizing Milky Way magnetic fields.

title: Revisiting ram pressure stripping in Wolf-Lundmark-Melotte: No evidence for stripped HI with LGLBS
comment: Accepted for publication to AJ; 6 pages, 4 figures
summary: We analyze HI 21-cm observations of the Local Group dwarf galaxy Wolf-Lundmark-Melotte (WLM) from the Local Group L-Band Survey to search for evidence of ram pressure stripping. While previous MeerKAT-16 observations of WLM showed evidence for off-galaxy atomic gas emission with a geometry suggestive of ram pressure stripping, our observations find no evidence for this stripped gas. We demonstrate that our observations would be sensitive to the claimed detections and suggest that an uncorrected observational flaw with the MeerKAT data led to the apparent off-galaxy emission. The lack of off-galaxy emission obviates the need for uncharacteristically high values of the density of the intergalactic medium in this region.

AI.tldr: Analysis of WLM dwarf galaxy HI 21-cm observations shows no evidence for ram pressure stripping, contradicting previous MeerKAT-16 findings, and attributing the earlier detection to an uncorrected observational flaw.
AI.motivation: To search for evidence of ram pressure stripping in the Local Group dwarf galaxy WLM and verify previous claims of off-galaxy atomic gas emission from MeerKAT-16 observations.
AI.method: Analyzed HI 21-cm observations of WLM from the Local Group L-Band Survey and assessed sensitivity to previously claimed detections of stripped gas.
AI.result: No evidence for stripped gas was found; observations were sufficiently sensitive to detect the claimed emission, suggesting the earlier detection was due to an uncorrected observational flaw.
AI.conclusion: The lack of off-galaxy emission removes the need to invoke uncharacteristically high intergalactic medium densities, and the previous claim was likely spurious.
